llm_text: I’ve had luck with a few practical moves that make the “effort over outcome” mindset stick. First, we make it part of onboarding — every new coach/volunteer hears the expectations from day one and signs a simple code of conduct that highlights praising effort, rotating roles, and giving private feedback. We run short, regular trainings (5–10 minute huddles or a quick role‑play) so people practice how to give constructive feedback and public shout‑outs. We also use visible reminders: a shout‑out board, monthly “effort awards” (nothing fancy — a certificate or small gift card), and sharing quick success stories in meetings so people see real examples of progress. Pairing newer volunteers with seasoned ones as mentors helps, and leaders are evaluated partly on how well they model these behaviors. When parents or coaches push back, I meet privately, explain how the approach protects everyone and improves retention, and offer concrete ways they can help; if someone keeps undermining it, we use the consequence ladder and involve neutral leadership. Consistency and making the mission — the kids’ growth/our service — more important than wins is what actually changes behavior. How has your group handled someone who refuses to play by the effort-first rules?
